title: The Marshmallow Test
text:
Starting in the late 1960s, Walter Mischel and his colleagues at Stanford University ran a simple experiment with preschoolers at the campus nursery school. A child sat at a table with a treat, often a marshmallow or a pretzel. The researcher explained that they were going to leave the room. If the child waited until the researcher came back, they would get two treats. If they could not wait, they could ring a bell and eat one right away.

Some children ate the treat almost at once. Others waited for many minutes. The most interesting finding was how they managed it. Children who succeeded often covered their eyes, sang, played with their hands, or imagined the marshmallow as a fluffy cloud rather than something tasty. Waiting was much easier when the treat was hidden than when it sat in plain view.

In a 1989 review in Science, Mischel, Yuichi Shoda and Monica Rodriguez summarized this work and reported that children who had waited longer were, years later, described by their parents as more competent adolescents and had higher SAT scores.

Those long-term links became famous. A 2018 study by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan, using a larger and more diverse sample, found them much weaker once family background and early abilities were taken into account.
lesson: Self-control is less about willpower than about strategy. Help children, and yourself, by changing what is in view and what you think about while waiting.
people: Walter Mischel, Yuichi Shoda, Monica Rodriguez
location: Bing Nursery School, Stanford University, Stanford, USA
source: Mischel, W., Shoda, Y., and Rodriguez, M. L. (1989). Delay of gratification in children. Science, 244(4907), 933-938.
caveat: The follow-up samples were small, and a 2018 replication found the link between waiting time and later achievement much weaker after controlling for family background.
